source_text: Idolum aliquamdiu retro non erat. priusquam huius moustri artifices ebullissent, sola templa et uacuae aedes eraut, sicut in hodiernum quibusdam locis uetustatis uestigia permanent. tamen idololatria agebatur, non in isto nomine, sed in isto opere. nam et hodie extra templum et sine idolo agi potest. at ubi artifices statuarum et imaginum et omnis generis simulacrorum diabolus saeculo intulit, rude illud negotium humanae calamitatis et nomen de idolis consecutum est et profectum. exinde iam caput facta est idololatriae ars omnis quae idolum quoquomodo edit. neque enim interest, an plastes effingat, an caelator exculpat, an phrygio detegat, quia nec de materia refert, an gypso, an coloribus, an lapide, an aere, an argento, an filo formetur idolum. quando enim et sine idolo idololatria fiat, utique, cum adest idolum, nihil interest, quale sit, qua de materia, qua de effigie, ne qui putet id solum idolum habendum, quod humana effigie sit consecratum. ad hoc necessaria est uocabuli interpretatio. εί̉δοςGraece formam sonat; ab eo per diminutionem εἵδωλον deductum; aeque apud nos forma formulam fecit. igitur omnis forma uel formula idolum se dici exposcit. inde idololatria omnis circa omne idolum famulatus et seruitus. inde et omnis idoli artifex eiusdem et unius est criminis, nisi parum idololatrian populus admisit, quia simulacrum uituli et non hominis sibi consecrauit.
thought_title: The origin and scope of idol-making
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that idolatry must be recognized beyond its open forms, and here he traces how the craft of making idols gave idolatry its name and made every maker of any idol guilty of the same crime.
pass_a_gloss: An idol did not exist for some time in the past. Before the craftsmen of this monster had bubbled up, only temples and empty shrines existed, just as in the present day in some places traces of antiquity remain. Nevertheless idolatry was being practiced, not in that name, but in that work. For even today it can be practiced outside a temple and without an idol. But when the devil introduced into the world craftsmen of statues and images and statues of every kind, that rough business of human calamity both obtained the name from idols and made progress. From then on every art which produces an idol in any way has become the head of idolatry. For it makes no difference whether a modeler fashions it, or an engraver carves it, or an embroiderer weaves it, because it does not matter regarding the material whether the idol is formed from gypsum, or from colors, or from stone, or from bronze, or from silver, or from thread. For when idolatry can happen even without an idol, certainly, when an idol is present, it makes no difference what kind it is, from what material, from what likeness, lest anyone think that only that idol must be considered which has been consecrated with a human likeness. For this the interpretation of the word is necessary. Eidos in Greek means form; from it by diminution eidolon is derived; equally among us forma made formula. Therefore every form or formula demands to be called an idol. Hence idolatry is every service and servitude around every idol. Hence also every maker of an idol is of the same and one crime, unless the people admitted idolatry too little because they consecrated to themselves a statue of a calf and not of a human.

choices.why: The source spelling 'moustri' is a variant of 'monstri'; rendering as 'monster' preserves the rhetorical force of idolatry as a monstrous thing.
The verb ebullio means to bubble up or boil forth; keeping the vivid metaphor preserves Tertullian's contemptuous tone about the emergence of idol craftsmen.
Rude means rough or unformed; 'rough business' keeps the sense of an unrefined, base trade, and 'business' captures negotium as an occupation or affair.

choices.term: caput facta est idololatriae ars omnis
choices.english: every art which produces an idol in any way has become the head of idolatry
choices.why: Caput means head or source; rendering as 'head' preserves the metaphor of idolatry as a body with idol-making as its chief part, matching the earlier argument that idolatry is the head of injustice.
The two near-synonyms emphasize total subservience; keeping both as 'service and servitude' preserves the rhetorical doubling.

choices.english: the people admitted idolatry too little
choices.why: Parum means too little; the ironic sense is that the people did not merely admit idolatry but fully committed it, so rendering literally preserves the sarcasm.
rejected: the people admitted idolatry only slightly

pass_b_english: There was a time when no idol existed. Before the craftsmen of this monster had arisen, temples stood empty and bare, and in some places the traces of that antiquity remain even today. Yet idolatry was already being practiced, not under that name, but in that deed. Even now it can be practiced outside a temple and without an idol.

But when the devil introduced into the world the craftsmen of statues and images and every kind of likeness, that rough business of human calamity took its name from idols and grew. From then on, every art that produces an idol in any way has become the head of idolatry.

It makes no difference whether a modeler shapes it, an engraver carves it, or an embroiderer weaves it, because the material does not matter either, whether the idol is formed from plaster, colors, stone, bronze, silver, or thread. Since idolatry can happen even without an idol, when an idol is present it makes no difference what kind it is, what material it is made of, or what likeness it bears. So no one should think that only something consecrated in human likeness is to be considered an idol.

For this, the interpretation of the word is necessary. Eidos in Greek means form; from it, by diminution, eidolon is derived. In the same way, among us forma produced formula. Therefore every form or formula demands to be called an idol. Hence idolatry is every service and servitude rendered to every idol. Hence every craftsman of an idol is guilty of one and the same crime, unless the people admitted idolatry too little because they consecrated for themselves the statue of a calf and not of a human being.
notes: The source contains the variant spellings 'moustri' for 'monstri', 'eraut' for 'erant', and 'idololatrian' for 'idololatriam'; these are likely scribal variants or OCR artifacts. The Greek terms εί̉δος and εἵδωλον are embedded in the Latin text.

problems.quote: before the craftsmen of this monster had bubbled up
problems.why: 'Bubbled up' is nonsensical for emergence of craftsmen.
problems.fix: Change to 'before the craftsmen of this monster had arisen'.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening sentence about the craftsmen, broke the long passage into shorter paragraphs at natural turns, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and qualification.
